primary_meaning: Jesus Christ as the sacrificial, redemptive Lamb—innocent and slain for sin, yet risen, victorious, enthroned, and worthy of worship.
primary_basis: John 1:29, 36 identifies Jesus as “the Lamb of God” who takes away the sin of the world.
Revelation 5:6-14 portrays the slain yet living Lamb as worthy to open the scroll and receive universal worship.
Revelation 7:9-17; 12:11; 13:8; 17:14; 19:7-9; 21:22-27; 22:1-3 develop the Lamb as redeemer, conqueror, bridegroom, judge, and divine ruler.
1 Peter 1:18-19 describes Christ as a spotless and unblemished lamb whose blood redeems believers.
Isaiah 53:7, read christologically in Acts 8:32-35, supplies the image of the innocent suffering servant led like a lamb to slaughter.
Exodus 12:1-32 and 1 Corinthians 5:7 connect Christ with the Passover lamb and deliverance through sacrificial blood.

alternatives.meaning: The Passover lamb specifically: Christ as the agent of a new exodus whose blood delivers from judgment and bondage.
The Isaianic suffering servant: Christ as innocent, submissive, and suffering on behalf of others.
The victorious apocalyptic Messiah: especially in Revelation, the Lamb is a conquering king, judge, and ruler whose victory comes through sacrificial death.
A representative sacrificial lamb without commitment to one exclusive Old Testament background, such as Passover, Isaiah 53, the daily temple offering, or other sacrifices.

In other contexts, lamb imagery can denote vulnerable or faithful people rather than Christ, or can be imitated deceptively by an anti-Christian power; these are contextual uses rather than the normal meaning of the title “the Lamb.”

notes: Christian interpretation overwhelmingly identifies the titular “Lamb,” especially in John and Revelation, with Jesus Christ. Debate concerns which scriptural sacrificial background is primary and whether sacrifice, Passover deliverance, suffering innocence, or apocalyptic victory receives the main emphasis; these readings are usually complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
